issues.legal_issue: Whether the stall-holders’ arrangement created a lease or only a licence depended on the parties’ intention, assessed from the agreement and, where needed, the surrounding circumstances and conduct.
material_facts: The written agreements were signed only by the stall-holders, and fresh agreements were executed when the market’s collection contractor changed.

The agreements called the daily payments “rent,” required only 24 hours’ notice for eviction after three days of non-payment, and allowed the landlord to require the stall-holder to vacate on 30 days’ notice.
The stalls were open and separated by low walls. Stall-holders could use them only during market hours, had to leave when the market closed, and could not enter them at night.
The owners were responsible for market cleaning, disinfection, closure, and compliance with municipal requirements, and needed access to the stalls to perform those duties.
The stall-holders had no right to use the stalls whenever they chose or to remain there overnight.
issues.conclusion: The parties intended to create licences, not leases; the word “rent” was used loosely to mean a fee.
issues.legal_principle: The decisive consideration in distinguishing a lease from a licence is the parties’ intention, determined from all relevant terms and, where there is no clear formal agreement, the circumstances and conduct. Exclusive possession is important but is not conclusive; exclusive possession coupled with an interest in the property points to a lease. A requirement to give notice before a licensee must vacate is not inconsistent with a licence, including under section 62(c) of the Indian Easements Act, 1882. The Court relied on Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. R. N. Kapoor, Errington v. Errington and Woods, Cobb v. Lane, Close v. Theatrical Properties Ltd. and Westby & Co. Ltd., Smith & Son v. The Assessment Committee for the Parish of Lambeth, and Vurum Subba Rao v. The Eluru Municipal Council.

rule.if: stall_occupation_classification_dispute and (use_limited_to_stated_hours and owners_retain_operational_control) and not stall_holder_has_property_interest

predicates.stall_occupation_classification_dispute: The parties dispute whether an arrangement for occupying a stall gives the occupant a lease or only a licence.
predicates.use_limited_to_stated_hours: The occupant may use the stall only during stated hours and must leave when the premises close.
predicates.owners_retain_operational_control: The owners retain responsibility for operating, maintaining, cleaning, or securing the premises and need access to the stall to perform those responsibilities.
predicates.stall_holder_has_property_interest: The occupant has an interest in the property in addition to the right to use the stall.

issues.definition: When a stall-occupation dispute involves use limited to stated hours and the owners retain operational control, the absence of a property interest means the arrangement is a licence rather than a lease.

issues.legal_issue: A requirement to give notice before an occupant must vacate, or the occupant’s exclusive use of a stall, does not by itself establish a lease.
material_facts: The agreements required notice before a stall-holder could be required to vacate, including 30 days’ notice when the landlord required the stall.
Each stall-holder had exclusive use of the stall during market hours, but could not use it at will, remain there overnight, or enter after the market closed.
The stall-holders’ use was subject to the owners’ continuing responsibilities for the market.
issues.conclusion: Neither the notice requirement nor exclusive use alone established a lease; exclusive possession would point to a lease if coupled with an interest in the property.
issues.legal_principle: The decisive consideration remains the parties’ intention. A contractual licence may require notice before termination or vacation, and section 62(c) of the Indian Easements Act, 1882 recognises that a licence may be revoked when a specified condition is fulfilled. Exclusive possession is not conclusive of a tenancy, though it is an important consideration; when coupled with an interest in the property it supports construing the arrangement as a lease. The Court relied on Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. R. N. Kapoor, Errington v. Errington and Woods, Cobb v. Lane, Close v. Theatrical Properties Ltd. and Westby & Co. Ltd., and Smith & Son v. The Assessment Committee for the Parish of Lambeth.

predicates.stall_occupation_classification_dispute: The parties dispute whether an arrangement for occupying a stall gives the occupant a lease or only a licence.
predicates.notice_required_before_vacating: The arrangement requires notice before the occupant can be required to vacate.
predicates.exclusive_use_of_stall: The occupant has exclusive use of the stall, whether or not that use is restricted in time or subject to the owners’ control.

issues.definition: In a stall-occupation classification dispute, a notice requirement or exclusive use of the stall, by itself, does not establish a lease.

issues.legal_issue: Surrounding circumstances may be considered to interpret an ambiguous written arrangement, including where the document relied on is signed only by the occupant.
material_facts: The agreements were written but signed only by the stall-holders, rather than being formal agreements signed by both parties.
The agreements described the daily payment as “rent,” while payment accrued from day to day and non-payment for three days could lead to eviction on 24 hours’ notice.
The parties disputed whether the written arrangements created a tenancy or a licence.
issues.conclusion: The surrounding circumstances could be considered to ascertain the real relationship between the parties and the meaning of “rent” in the agreements.
issues.legal_principle: Section 92 of the Indian Evidence Act excludes oral evidence to contradict or vary the terms of a written instrument, but its sixth proviso permits surrounding circumstances to be considered to ascertain the meaning of words in the instrument. Where the terms are unclear and the documents are not formal agreements between the parties, the parties’ circumstances and conduct may also be considered in determining their intention.

predicates.stall_occupation_classification_dispute: The parties dispute whether an arrangement for occupying a stall gives the occupant a lease or only a licence.
predicates.written_terms_ambiguous: The written terms do not clearly identify the nature of the parties’ relationship.
predicates.agreement_signed_only_by_occupant: The document relied on as the agreement is signed by the occupant but not by the other party.

issues.definition: Where a stall-occupation dispute concerns unclear written terms in a document signed only by the occupant, the surrounding circumstances may be considered to interpret the arrangement.
